case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 7-3-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4491 of 2002).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain, CJ: This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 7-3-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4491 of 2002 discharging the Rule and affirming the judgment and decree dated 8-7-2002 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Natore Sadar, Natore in SCC Suit No.2 of 1996 decreeing the suit. 

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this civil appeal, in a nutshell, are: 
The respondent herein as the plaintiff instituted SSC Suit No.2 of 1996 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Natore for eviction of the defendants alleging, inter-alia, that the defendants were the tenants of the disputed homestead under Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury as monthly ejectable tenants at a rental of Taka 400 per month. There was an agreement that the rent should be paid within the first week of the next month. Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury decided to sell the disputed property and accordingly, the plaintiff decided to purchase the same at a consideration of Taka 51,000. Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury agreed with the same. On 1-5-1977, executing Bainanama said Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury received Taka 46,000 and delivered possession of the premises with the land in favour of the plaintiff. There was also an agreement with the defendants that after registration of the sale deed, they would quit the suit premises after issuance of one month notice by the plaintiff. But said Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury denied executing and register the sale deed on the basis of the said Bainanama. Accordingly, the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.167 of 1984 for specific performance of contract and got decree and obtained the kabala deed registered through the Court on 26-8-1991. The defendants after taking lease of the disputed property from Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury failed to pay rent regularly. After purchase, the plaintiff requested the defendants to pay rent but the defendants did not pay any heed. The defendants are habitual defaulters in payment of rent. The suit premises are necessary for the purpose of plaintiff's own use and occupation. In such circumstances, the plaintiff issued notice through his engaged lawyer on 6-6-1996 under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act which was duly served upon the defendants on 9-6-1996 and 10-6-1996 with the request to quit and vacate the premises. But the defendants did not vacate the suit premises and hence the plaintiff was constrained to file the above suit. 

3. By way of amendment of the plaint, the plaintiff added that the Bainanamas dated 14-5-1983 as executed by Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury in favour of defendant Nos.1 and 2 are forged, fraudulent and those have been created for using against the plaintiff in the present suit. The defendants were fully aware of those Bainanamas of the plaintiff and, as such, there is no reason for them to take Bainanamas from Nuruzzaman. 

4. Defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint of the suit, contending, inter-alia, that the suit was not maintainable; it was barred by waiver, estoppel, and acquiescence and limitation. Their specific case, in short, is that defendant No.1 joined as Lecturer of Naogaon Degree College in 1962. Thereafter, he joined as Professor of Natore NS College. He started living in a rented house along with his wife situated at the northern side of the Madrasha. Mr AKM Naimul Ahsan, nephew of defendant No.2, got admission in Natore NS College. On the other hand, a son of Abdur Rouf Chowdhury of Chowdhury Bari also got admission in the said Natore NS College. Consequently, they became friends. At one stage, son of Abdur Rouf Chowdhury requested defendant No.1 to live in the disputed house which is undivided and belonged to Chowdhury family. Defendant No.1 was informed that the suit house is under care of Safia Mohabbat and that deeds to be reconstructed because of its dilapidated condition Abdur Rouf Chowdhury also informed him that defendant No.1 could live therein if he so desired by reconstructing the said house. He also asserted that after effecting final partition if Shafia Mohabbat gets the said homestead and decides to sell the same and then defendant No.1 can purchase the same. Accordingly, spending Taka 13,000, defendant No.1 reconstructed the disputed homestead. It has been also mentioned that the father-in-law of defendant No.1 i.e. the father of defendant No.2 Zahurul Islam was the founder Principal of Natore NS College. One Zamir Ali, Nayeb of Chowdhury family, disclosed to brother of defendant No.2 Sirajul Islam that Nuruzamman Khan Chowdhury has got the disputed premises by way of partition. Accordingly, Sirajul Islam, brother of defendant No.2 told defendant No.1 that said Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury would sell the said homestead. Learning this the defendants decided to purchase the said homestead and it was agreed with Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury that the suit property and structures thereon would be sold at a consideration of Taka 50,000. On 14-5-1983 said Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury executed 2 bainanamas on receipt of Taka 2500 + 2500 in favour of defendant Nos.1 and 2. Thereafter, defendant No.1 on 16-1-1985 got kabala deed registered on the basis of the said bainanamas in respect of 0.04 acre of land and premises thereon. Defendant No.2 got registration of the 0.04 acre of land from said Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury on 2-2-1985. That was done within the knowledge of the plaintiff. Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury had been living at Rajshahi Town, that is why the kabala deeds were registered at Rajshahi. The defendants are not monthly ejectable tenants under Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury and they did not pay any rent to him. Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury did not execute any bainanama in favour of the plaintiff. After purchase the defendants mutated their names in the khatian and paid rent to the Government. The kabala deed dated 26-8-1991 as obtained by the plaintiff is fraudulent because Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury transferred the suit property long before execution and registration of the deed of the plaintiff and by the said kabala deed dated 26-8-1991 the plaintiff did not acquire any title. The plaintiff has got no right, title and possession in the suit premises. As such the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 8-7-2002 by the trial Court, the defendants preferred a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.4491 of 2002. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 7-3-2007 discharged the Rule. 

6. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the defendants as the leave-petitioners have filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1049 of 2007 before this Division, in which, leave was granted on 15-10-2008, resulting in Civil Appeal No. 8 of 2009.

7. Mr Farid Ahmed, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that there is nothing on record that after transferring the suit property to the respondent, Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury made any attornment saying that the plaintiff purchased the suit property and, as such, the defendants are not liable to pay rent to the plaintiff-respondent and, as such, the suit for eviction of the defendants as monthly tenants of the plaintiff is not maintainable and that the High Court Division and the SCC Court decreed the suit ignoring this aspect of this case and, as such, the impugned judgment should be set-aside. He further submits that the High Court Division and the trial Court committed error of law in decreeing the suit for ejectment of monthly tenants inasmuch as there is nothing in the materials on record that the defendants are the monthly tenants under the plaintiff-respondents. He then submits that the High Court Division and the trial Court should have held that the instant suit was not maintainable without a prayer for partition. He lastly submits that the appellants were in permissive possession of the suit property and that the admitted owner Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury allowed the appellants to possess the suit property and that Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury transferred the suit property to the defendant-appellants on 2-2-1985 and 16-1-1985 on the basis of two deeds. As such, the defendant-appellants acquired valid title to the suit land and that on the other hand, the plaintiff claimed title on the basis of deed of sale dated 26-8-1991 executed and registered through the Court in pursuance of the decree passed in Title Suit No.167 of 1984 and the defendants are not tenants under the plaintiff-respondent and, as such, the judgments of the High Court Division and the trial Court should be set-aside. 

8. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Senior Advocate; appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that the decree passed in Other Class Suit No.167 of 1984 was upheld by the Appellate Division and, as such, the defendant-appellants cannot claim title to the suit land on the basis of their alleged purchase dated 16-1-1985 and 2-2-1985 and, as such, no interference is called for. He further submits that defendant No.1 in his evidence admitted that he was a tenant under Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury and therefore, the defendants have become tenants under the plaintiff after his purchase of the disputed property and, as such, the impugned judgment should not be interfered with. He then submits that the deeds of sale dated 16-1-1985 and 2-2-1985 are hit by the doctrine of lis pendens and that the defendants are bound by the decree passed in Other Class Suit No.167 of 1984 and, as such, the defendants did not acquire any title to the suit land. 

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment and order delivered by the High Court Division and the materials on record. 

10. Before addressing the submissions made by the learned Senior Advocates of respective parties, we should have a glance over the submissions, on which, leave was granted. The submissions are quoted below: 
"The defendants were in permissive possession in the suit property and admittedly owner Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury allowed them to possess the suit property and accordingly while owning and. possessing the same, said Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury transferred the same to the defendant petitioners on 2-2-1985 and 16-1-1985 i.e. on the basis of those Kabala deeds the defendant petitioners acquired valid title to the suit land. On the other hand, the plaintiffs claimed title on the basis of the Kabala deed dated 26-8-1991 as executed and registered by the court in pursuance of the decree passed in Title suit No.267 of 1994 [sic/ So it could not be said that the defendants were tenants under the plaintiffs, so the instant suit for eviction of the defendant petitioners, treating them as monthly tenant is not maintainable, the courts below committed an error of law in assuming that the defendants are tenants of the plaintiff, so they are ejectable tenants in a suit for eviction under the provision of Small Causes Courts Act. 
There is nothing in the materials on record that after transferring the suit property, Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury made any attornment saying that as the plaintiff purchased the suit property, the defendants are liable to pay rent in favour of the plaintiff. In absence of any such asttornment the suit for eviction of the defendants as monthly tenants of the plaintiff is not maintainable. Both the courts below ignoring that aspect of the matter decreed the suit which has caused total failure of justice. 
Both the Courts below committed an error of law in decreeing the suit for ejectment of monthly tenants inasmuch as there is nothing in the materials on record that the defendants are monthly tenants under the plaintiff. 
Both the courts below ought to have held that the instant suit was not maintainable without a prayer for partition." 

11. The trial Court in clear terms stated that both the parties admitted that the suit land and the premises standing thereon belonged to Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury. The learned SCC Judge noted that DW 1 in his cross-examination stated that as soon as repairment of the disputed house was completed Chowdhury Shahab told him that now the rent was to be fixed. From the aforesaid admission of the DW 1, it appears that the defendants were, in fact, tenants under Nuruzzaman Khan Cowdhury. The trial Court came to the finding that Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury could not transfer the disputed property after Other Class Suit No.167 of 1984 was filed without prior permission of the Court and that by the alleged transfer during pendency of the suit, any plaintiff-respondent was not affected in any way. The trial Court noted that Other Class Suit No.167 of 1984 was decreed on contest on 1-7-1990 and that pursuant to the aforesaid decree, a deed of sale was registered on 26-8-1991 in favour of the plaintiff-respondent in respect of the suit property measuring 0.89 acre of land. The trial Court came to the finding that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served upon the defendants determining tenancy and that the defendants did not state anything about the aforesaid notice. The trial Court then held that though Nuruzzaman Khan Chowdhury entered into a contract to sell the disputed property to the plaintiff-respondent, he sold the said property to the defendants for illegal gain. The trial Court came to the finding that the defendants were habitual defaulters and, as such, the plaintiff-respondent was entitled to get a decree for eviction of the defendants from the disputed premises. 

12. The High Court Division while concurring with the judgment and decree passed by the SCC Court came to the finding that the suit premises is identical to the land allegedly purchased by the defendants on the basis of deeds of sale dated 16-1-1985 and 2-2-1985. The High Court Division found that the deeds of sale of the defendants were illegal as per doctrine of lis pendens as both the aforesaid deeds were executed and registered during pendency of Other Class Suit No.167 of 1984. The High Court Division came to the finding that in the SCC Suit there was no scope to question whether the bainapatra dated 1-5-1977 in favour of the plaintiff-respondent was genuine or not as Other Class Suit No.167 of 1984 for enforcement of the said bainapatra was decreed. The High Court Division came to the finding that the Court of Small Causes was entitled to consider the question of title incidentally and that in the instant suit, the question of title was not involved. The decree passed in Other Class Suit No.167 of 1984 was affirmed by the appellate Court and however, the High Court Division set-aside the concurrent findings of the Courts below and dismissed the suit. But the Appellate Division set-aside the judgment and order of the High Court Division and restored the judgments of the trial Court and the appellate Court and, as such, there was no scope to question the title of the plaintiff-respondent. 

13. The findings of the High Court Division and the SCC Court are based on proper appreciation of evidence on record. It is contended that the defendants were not parties to Other Class Suit No.167 of 1984 and, as such, the deeds of sale dated 16-1-1985 and 2-2-1985 in their names are not hit by the doctrine of lis pendens. In order to resolve the issue, it is necessary to quote section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act as under: 
"Transfer of property pending suit relating thereto—During the pendency in any Court in Bangladesh of any suit or proceeding which is not collusive and in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made therein, except under the authority of the Court and on such terms as it may impose. 
Explanation—For the purposes of this section, the pendency of a suit or proceeding shall be deemed to commence from the date of the presentation of the plaint or the institution of the proceeding in a Court of competent jurisdiction, and to continue until the suit or proceeding has been disposed of by a final decree or order and complete satisfaction or discharge of such decree or order has been obtained, or has become unobtainable by reason of the expiration of any period of limitation prescribed for the execution thereof by any law for the time being in force." 

14. Having gone through the provision of section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, we find that during pendency of the suit, the property in question cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit so as to affect the right of any other party of that suit under any decree or order which may be made in that suit without prior permission of the Court. 

15. The explanation appended to this section states that lis pendens shall operate from the date of presentation of the plaint or institution of the proceeding in any Court of competent jurisdiction and shall continue till the suit or proceeding is finally disposed of. 

16. Reliance may be placed on the case of Atar Ali vs Abed Ali, 5 DLR 267, where it has been observed, "The objection in the case is that the lease in favour of the petitioner is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, it having been executed during pendency of a contentious suit. Where a transfer is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, the transferee is not entitled to hold his title against a party to the suit sought to be affected by the transfer. That appears clearly from these words in section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. 
As his lease is hit by this section, the petitioner has no defence to make against the plaintiff. It is not disputed before me that a suit for specific performance of a contract for a lease amounts to a suit in which the right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question. There are decisions, such as Johar Mull Bhatra vs Jatindra Nath Bose, 34 CLI 79, where it has been held that a suit for specific performance of a contract operated as lis pendens." 

17. From the case cited above it appears that the doctrine of lis pendens does not make alienations made during pendency of a suit void but only that such alienation will not affect the rights of other parties to the suit. It means that the purchaser pendente lite is bound by the result of the litigation. It is immaterial whether subsequent transferee is a party to that suit or not. 

18. It is contended that the defendants did not attorn the plaintiff as landlord and, as such, the High Court Division as well as the SCC Court committed error of law in holding that the defendants are tenants under the plaintiff. Admittedly, notice terminating the tenancy was issued on the defendants on 6-6-1986 and the same was served upon the defendants on 10-6-1996. The defendants did not deny that they had not received the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 10-6-1996 and did not controvert the said notice by giving any reply thereto. Even in their written statement, the defendants did not say a single word against the notice issued on them under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

19. In the light of the findings made before, we are of the view that the ground taken in this appeal in respect of attornment by the appellants falls through. 

20. In the case of Appollo Zipper India Limited vs W Newman and Company Limited (2018) 6 SCC 744 when the appellant sent a quit notice dated 17-5-2012 to the respondent under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act terminating the tenancy and calling upon the respondent to pay arrears of rent and vacate the suit premises, despite receipt of the quite notice, they did not reply to it. The Supreme Court of Indian held that the respondent ought to have replied to the notice at the first available opportunity, which they failed to do so. It amounts to waiver on their part to challenge the validity or infirmity of the quit notice including the ownership issue raised therein. 

21. In the case of Mahendra Raghunathrlas Gupta vs Vishwanath Bhikaji Mogul, AIR 1997 (SC) 2437 the Supreme Court of Indian held that it is well settled that a transferee of the landlord with all the rights and liabilities of the transferee landlord steps into the shoes of the landlord with all the rights and liabilities of the transferor landlord in respect of the subsisting tenancy. The section does not require the transfer of the right of the landlord can take effect only if the tenant attorns to him. Attomment by the tenant is not necessary to confer validity of the transfer of the landlord's rights. Since attornment by the tenant is not required a notice under section 106 in terms of the old terms of lease by the transferor landlord would be proper and so also the suit for ejectment. 

22. Attornment would, however, be desirable as it means the acknowledgement of relation of a tenant to a new landlord. It also implies continuity of tenancy. 

23. In the case of Selina Begum, vs Azizun Nessa, 6 BLC (AD) 115, this Division has held that attornment by the tenant is not necessary to confer validity of the landlord's right under the subsisting tenancy. The tenancy continues and the default of the defendant in payment of rent makes her liable for eviction. 

24. From the cases cited above, it appears that attornment by tenant as not necessary to confer validity of the transfer of the landlord's rights. Since attornment by the tenant is not required a notice 106 of the Transfer of Property Act in terms of lease by transferor land landlord would be proper and so also the suit for ejectment. Attornment would, however, be desirable as it means the acknowledgement of relation of a tenant to new landlord. It also implies continuity of tenancy. 

In the light of the findings made before, we do not find any substance in this appeal. Accordingly, this civil appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. 

End.
